@graph.name: County Leader’s Guide to Schemas
@graph.abstract: You do not need to design a schema. You need to ask whether the rules behind our information are stable, understandable, and compatible with the systems we already use.
@graph.description: A plain-language leadership companion to the County Leader’s Guide to Data. Created for Marin Learn demonstration and discussion; illustrative workflows are not statements of County policy.

audience.audienceType: County executives, department directors, and program leaders

@graph.name: Learning objectives
@graph.description: Practical leadership skills for recognizing schemas and asking for safe, dependable connections between County systems.

@graph.name: Explain a schema as an agreement about information, not a technical product
Recognize when similar fields do not describe the same fact
Ask whether a schema is stable, documented, and managed through changes
Recognize what systems need to exchange information reliably
Separate schema compatibility from permission to share sensitive data
Identify who is responsible for business definitions and their changes
Ask vendors to demonstrate an integration with a named existing application
Use plain-language schema questions in leadership decisions
Choose a small, testable cross-system handoff before expanding
A Schema Is an Agreement, Not a Technology
@graph.abstract: A schema is an agreed description of information: its names, meanings, allowed values, and connections. Leaders do not need to write one; they need to ask whether it exists.

@graph.name: The Same Label Can Mean Two Different Things
@graph.abstract: Matching column names do not guarantee matching meanings. Two departments can report the same label while counting or describing different things.

@graph.name: One Work Order, Two Systems
@graph.abstract: A facilities work-order system and a finance system may describe the same job in different ways. Integration succeeds when the meaning and record identity are reconciled.

@graph.name: Stable Does Not Mean Frozen
@graph.abstract: A stable schema can evolve. The key is that definitions are documented, changes are communicated, and existing connections do not break without a plan.

@graph.name: A Record Needs a Reliable Identity
@graph.abstract: A stable record identifier helps applications recognize the same work order, case, or transaction across handoffs; matching labels or names is not enough.

@graph.name: The Business Must Own the Meaning
@graph.abstract: Program leaders and data stewards need to agree on business definitions, while technology teams implement and maintain those definitions in connected systems.

@graph.name: A Shared Schema Is Not Permission to Share Everything
@graph.abstract: Compatible schemas make appropriate exchange easier, but privacy, security, purpose, and authorization still govern which data may actually be shared.

@graph.name: Do Not Buy a Promise of Integration
@graph.abstract: Ask vendors to show actual field definitions, change management, and a sample exchange with a named County application before treating integration as proven.

@graph.name: The 60-Second Schema Check
@graph.abstract: Seven plain-language questions let leaders identify schema and integration risks before a purchase, report, dashboard, or cross-department handoff.

@graph.name: Start With One Handoff, Not a Countywide Rewrite
@graph.abstract: Pick two systems and a handful of important fields, test sample records, record the differences, and agree on owners before scaling the connection.

@graph.name: What to Say at the Next Meeting
@graph.abstract: The leadership skill is not schema engineering. It is asking for documented meaning, a stable connection, clear ownership, and a concrete demonstration.

County Leader’s Guide to Schemas — Reading Material
@graph.abstract: A practical County leadership guide to shared data definitions, stable change, safe integration, vendor questions, and one small first project.

@graph.name: A department head asks what a schema is. Which answer is most useful?
@graph.text: A department head asks what a schema is. Which answer is most useful?
@graph.marin:hint: Think about the agreement behind the fields, rather than a product that displays them.
@graph.marin:explanation: A schema makes the meaning, structure, and rules of information explicit.

@graph.text: A list of computers that store the department’s records.
@graph.marin:feedback: This describes infrastructure, not the agreed meanings and rules of the records.

@graph.text: An agreed description of what information means and how it is organized.
@graph.marin:feedback: This is the core idea: a schema describes fields, allowed values, and relationships.

@graph.text: A dashboard displaying the latest performance results.
@graph.marin:feedback: A dashboard displays information; a schema defines how information is represented.

@graph.text: The software contract governing vendor support.
@graph.marin:feedback: A vendor contract may address schemas, but it is not itself the definition of the data.

@graph.name: Two County applications can use the same field name while giving it different meanings.
@graph.text: Two County applications can use the same field name while giving it different meanings.
@graph.marin:hint: Consider how two teams might count repeat visits.
@graph.marin:explanation: Shared labels are not proof of shared definitions.

@graph.text: True
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. One “People Served” field can count unique people while another counts visits.

@graph.text: False
@graph.marin:feedback: The same label does not guarantee the same definition. The values may count different things.

@graph.name: One program reports 400 people served, counting each person once. Another reports 600, counting visits. What should leadership establish before comparing the numbers?
@graph.text: One program reports 400 people served, counting each person once. Another reports 600, counting visits. What should leadership establish before comparing the numbers?
@graph.marin:hint: Separate a measure’s label from its counting rule.
@graph.marin:explanation: A comparison is trustworthy only when the underlying definitions are clear.

@graph.text: Whether both reports have the same logo.
@graph.marin:feedback: Visual consistency has no bearing on how the figures were counted.

@graph.text: Whether both reports were exported on the same day.
@graph.marin:feedback: Timing matters for reporting but does not resolve the underlying different counting rules.

@graph.text: Whether both programs mean the same thing by “served.”
@graph.marin:feedback: The counting definitions must be reconciled before comparisons or totals are meaningful.

@graph.text: Whether both departments use spreadsheets.
@graph.marin:feedback: The file format does not determine the meaning of the measures.

@graph.name: Which items would help another department understand a system’s schema? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: Which items would help another department understand a system’s schema? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: Think about what helps someone interpret records after they leave the source application.
@graph.marin:explanation: Meaning, allowed values, and stewardship are more useful for integration than visual design details.

@graph.text: A plain-language description of what each important field means.
@graph.marin:feedback: Definitions help teams interpret the same facts consistently.

@graph.text: A list of allowed status values and what they signify.
@graph.marin:feedback: Allowed values prevent ambiguous translations across systems.

@graph.text: The person or group responsible for changes to those definitions.
@graph.marin:feedback: An owner makes the agreement maintainable over time.

@graph.text: The color palette used for the application’s homepage.
@graph.marin:feedback: Visual branding does not define what a data field means.

@graph.name: A system that can export a CSV file is automatically compatible with another system’s data definitions.
@graph.text: A system that can export a CSV file is automatically compatible with another system’s data definitions.
@graph.marin:hint: Consider the difference between moving values and interpreting them.
@graph.marin:explanation: A file export is useful but does not by itself establish semantic interoperability.

@graph.text: True
@graph.marin:feedback: Exporting a CSV moves values, but does not guarantee that IDs, statuses, or definitions match.

@graph.text: False
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. Files can transfer records while the meaning and identity of their fields still differ.

@graph.name: Facilities reports that a repair is “Closed.” Finance reports that its invoice is “Paid.” What is the soundest conclusion?
@graph.text: Facilities reports that a repair is “Closed.” Finance reports that its invoice is “Paid.” What is the soundest conclusion?
@graph.marin:hint: Identify what event each status actually describes.
@graph.marin:explanation: A shared report needs a documented interpretation of both the work state and the payment state.

@graph.text: They mean the same thing because both indicate completion.
@graph.marin:feedback: The completion of work and payment of an invoice are distinct events.

@graph.text: The County should stop using either status.
@graph.marin:feedback: Both statuses may be useful in their respective systems.

@graph.text: The two meanings should be mapped before a combined report is trusted.
@graph.marin:feedback: A documented translation preserves what each system actually records.

@graph.text: The finance system should always replace the facilities system’s status.
@graph.marin:feedback: No one system’s status should silently overwrite a different business meaning.

@graph.name: Which best demonstrates that an application has a stable schema?
@graph.text: Which best demonstrates that an application has a stable schema?
@graph.marin:hint: Think about how systems stay dependable while programs change.
@graph.marin:explanation: Controlled, communicated change is the practical meaning of a stable schema.

@graph.text: Fields and statuses are never changed, even when a program evolves.
@graph.marin:feedback: Refusing every change can make a schema obsolete.

@graph.text: Any developer can add fields without notifying other teams.
@graph.marin:feedback: Unannounced changes create integration and reporting risk.

@graph.text: The vendor promises that all integrations will work indefinitely.
@graph.marin:feedback: Promises without documented change and testing practices are not enough.

@graph.text: Definitions are documented, changes are versioned, and affected connections are tested.
@graph.marin:feedback: Stability means predictable, managed changes—not permanent immobility.

@graph.name: A truly stable schema should never add a new field or change a permitted value.
@graph.text: A truly stable schema should never add a new field or change a permitted value.
@graph.marin:hint: Consider what happens when a program introduces a legitimate new status.
@graph.marin:explanation: Versioning, communication, and testing allow schemas to evolve responsibly.

@graph.text: True
@graph.marin:feedback: A schema can remain stable while evolving through documented, coordinated changes.

@graph.text: False
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. Stability is about predictable change and compatibility, not forbidding change.

@graph.name: A vendor will add “Waiting for Customer” as a new request status. Which actions should precede rollout? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: A vendor will add “Waiting for Customer” as a new request status. Which actions should precede rollout? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: Focus on meaning, dependencies, and communication.
@graph.marin:explanation: A schema change needs a definition, impact assessment, and a coordinated rollout.

@graph.text: Define when staff should use the new status.
@graph.marin:feedback: Without a definition, staff and reports may interpret the value differently.

@graph.text: Identify dashboards and connected systems expecting only the old statuses.
@graph.marin:feedback: Dependencies must be checked before a new value breaks their assumptions.

@graph.text: Test the change and tell affected teams what to expect.
@graph.marin:feedback: Testing and communication make the change manageable.

@graph.text: Keep the change undocumented so staff are not overwhelmed.
@graph.marin:feedback: Hiding the change is precisely how silent breakage begins.

@graph.name: What is the primary value of a stable work-order identifier when connecting Facilities and Finance?
@graph.text: What is the primary value of a stable work-order identifier when connecting Facilities and Finance?
@graph.marin:hint: Think about identifying a specific record when different systems use different labels.
@graph.marin:explanation: Stable identifiers support correct matching but do not replace quality controls.

@graph.text: It automatically grants Finance access to every facilities record.
@graph.marin:feedback: Identifiers do not grant authorization.

@graph.text: It helps both systems link activity to the correct work order.
@graph.marin:feedback: Reliable identity supports matching the same work across separate records.

@graph.text: It guarantees every invoice amount is correct.
@graph.marin:feedback: An ID helps matching, not the accuracy of amounts.

@graph.text: It eliminates the need to explain status values.
@graph.marin:feedback: Status definitions still need to be reconciled.

@graph.name: Facilities uses WO-2047 and Finance uses PAY-990 for related work. What would be most useful?
@graph.text: Facilities uses WO-2047 and Finance uses PAY-990 for related work. What would be most useful?
@graph.marin:hint: Two systems may assign different identifiers without either being wrong.
@graph.marin:explanation: A documented and tested crosswalk or shared key is the practical solution.

@graph.text: An approved, tested method to link the corresponding records.
@graph.marin:feedback: A reliable mapping reconciles different identifiers without guessing.

@graph.text: A rule that identical street names always mean identical jobs.
@graph.marin:feedback: Names and addresses can recur and are not unique proof of identity.

@graph.text: Removing the IDs so users see only descriptions.
@graph.marin:feedback: Removing stable identifiers makes reliable matching harder.

@graph.text: Reporting only records whose identifiers look similar.
@graph.marin:feedback: Similar-looking codes are not proof that records match.

@graph.name: Who should determine what “Successfully Referred” means for a County program?
@graph.text: Who should determine what “Successfully Referred” means for a County program?
@graph.marin:hint: Consider who understands the program’s work and who implements it in software.
@graph.marin:explanation: The business owns the definition; technology and other partners help keep it usable and safe.

@graph.text: Only the application vendor, because it owns the software.
@graph.marin:feedback: Vendor knowledge is useful, but County business meaning needs program governance.

@graph.text: Only the server administrator, because the field is stored on a server.
@graph.marin:feedback: Technical stewardship is not the same as business definition.

@graph.text: Program leadership with appropriate data, technology, and policy partners.
@graph.marin:feedback: Business and technical teams should jointly maintain the agreed meaning.

@graph.text: Whichever employee entered the most recent record.
@graph.marin:feedback: One data entry should not redefine the meaning for everyone.

@graph.name: A cross-department data handoff has inconsistent meanings. Who should participate in resolving it? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: A cross-department data handoff has inconsistent meanings. Who should participate in resolving it? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: Consider who knows the meaning, the connection, and the sharing constraints.
@graph.marin:explanation: A dependable agreement needs business, technical, and relevant oversight perspectives.

@graph.text: The program teams that use and interpret the data.
@graph.marin:feedback: They understand the business decisions behind the fields.

@graph.text: Technology and integration staff who maintain the systems.
@graph.marin:feedback: They can implement and test an agreed translation.

@graph.text: Appropriate privacy or security reviewers for the proposed exchange.
@graph.marin:feedback: They can review whether the planned movement of information is permitted and protected.

@graph.text: Only the department with the larger software budget.
@graph.marin:feedback: Budget size does not establish the authoritative meaning of shared fields.

@graph.name: Two systems can have compatible schemas even when sharing every available field between them would be inappropriate.
@graph.text: Two systems can have compatible schemas even when sharing every available field between them would be inappropriate.
@graph.marin:hint: Separate technical ability from policy and permitted use.
@graph.marin:explanation: Schema compatibility is not authorization to transfer sensitive or unnecessary data.

@graph.text: True
@graph.marin:feedback: Correct. Compatibility explains how information could be exchanged; authorization controls what should be exchanged.

@graph.text: False
@graph.marin:feedback: A compatible format does not override privacy, purpose, or access restrictions.

@graph.name: A receiving program needs referral status but not full case details. Which design choices are appropriate? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: A receiving program needs referral status but not full case details. Which design choices are appropriate? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: Evaluate both meaning and minimum necessary information.
@graph.marin:explanation: The safest reliable integration moves clearly defined, authorized fields rather than entire records by default.

@graph.text: Share only the status fields needed for the approved purpose.
@graph.marin:feedback: This keeps the exchange focused on the receiving team’s actual need.

@graph.text: Confirm the purpose, authorization, and applicable protections.
@graph.marin:feedback: Even a small transfer requires the right governance and safeguards.

@graph.text: Document how the shared status values will be interpreted.
@graph.marin:feedback: The recipient needs to understand what Accepted, Declined, or Pending means.

@graph.text: Copy the whole case history because it is easier to implement.
@graph.marin:feedback: Technical convenience does not justify moving unrelated sensitive fields.

@graph.name: A vendor says, “Our system integrates with anything.” What should a County leader ask next?
@graph.text: A vendor says, “Our system integrates with anything.” What should a County leader ask next?
@graph.marin:hint: A good next question turns a broad claim into observable evidence.
@graph.marin:explanation: Integration should be demonstrated using actual fields, meanings, and updates for the intended handoff.

@graph.text: “Can you demonstrate how key fields and statuses map to our named application?”
@graph.marin:feedback: A concrete, application-specific mapping is stronger evidence than a generic claim.

@graph.text: “Is your product logo customizable?”
@graph.marin:feedback: Branding does not demonstrate data compatibility.

@graph.text: “Can you promise never to change the system?”
@graph.marin:feedback: The objective is managed change, not a frozen product.

@graph.text: “Can you install it before the integration is tested?”
@graph.marin:feedback: Deployment ahead of testing increases avoidable risk.

@graph.name: Which vendor answer signals the greatest integration concern?
@graph.text: Which vendor answer signals the greatest integration concern?
@graph.marin:hint: Compare what is proven about the data with what is merely promised about export.
@graph.marin:explanation: The concerning response assumes compatibility without any evidence of definitions or matching.

@graph.text: “We can provide field definitions before the test.”
@graph.marin:feedback: Documented field meanings are a positive starting point.

@graph.text: “We need to review your existing system’s identifiers first.”
@graph.marin:feedback: Reviewing the target system is an appropriate step.

@graph.text: “We will test how changes affect your connected reports.”
@graph.marin:feedback: Dependency testing helps protect continuity.

@graph.text: “We export files, so matching fields and record IDs will take care of themselves.”
@graph.marin:feedback: Export alone does not resolve meaning, identity, or update behavior.

@graph.name: Which questions belong in a quick leadership schema review? Select all that apply.
@graph.text: Which questions belong in a quick leadership schema review? Select all that apply.
@graph.marin:hint: Focus on reliability, shared meaning, and demonstrated fit.
@graph.marin:explanation: Leadership can ask strong schema questions without becoming a technical reviewer.

@graph.text: “Does it have a documented, stable schema?”
@graph.marin:feedback: This checks whether a reliable agreement exists.

@graph.text: “Who tests and communicates field changes?”
@graph.marin:feedback: This checks whether the agreement remains dependable.

@graph.text: “Can someone show how it fits the other application’s schema?”
@graph.marin:feedback: This asks for evidence of real compatibility.

@graph.text: “Can we avoid documenting the data until after launch?”
@graph.marin:feedback: Skipping documentation postpones the problem instead of addressing it.

@graph.name: A countywide integration proposal seems complicated. What is the strongest first demonstration?
@graph.text: A countywide integration proposal seems complicated. What is the strongest first demonstration?
@graph.marin:hint: Which approach produces useful evidence with the smallest bounded effort?
@graph.marin:explanation: An early, constrained test reveals the real schema and governance work before scope expands.

@graph.text: Buy a replacement for every participating system immediately.
@graph.marin:feedback: A large purchase is not required to establish whether definitions can connect.

@graph.text: Choose two systems, a few key fields, and realistic approved test records.
@graph.marin:feedback: A focused handoff exposes mismatches early and establishes ownership.

@graph.text: Wait until all departments agree on every term they use.
@graph.marin:feedback: Countywide perfection is unnecessary before testing one relevant connection.

@graph.text: Publish a dashboard before confirming how fields match.
@graph.marin:feedback: Presentation should not get ahead of reliable definitions.

@graph.name: An integration team reports that the two systems use “Closed” differently. What leadership response best supports a sound project?
@graph.text: An integration team reports that the two systems use “Closed” differently. What leadership response best supports a sound project?
@graph.marin:hint: Consider how leaders can reward transparency and turn a problem into a decision.
@graph.marin:explanation: Surfacing a mismatch before launch is useful evidence, provided the team owns its resolution.

@graph.text: “Hide the difference so the launch date does not slip.”
@graph.marin:feedback: Concealing a known mismatch puts reporting and decisions at risk.

@graph.text: “Use the definition from whichever vendor costs more.”
@graph.marin:feedback: Price does not settle business meaning.

@graph.text: “Document the difference, assign an owner, and show how it will be handled.”
@graph.marin:feedback: Making the mismatch visible creates a manageable decision and follow-up.

@graph.text: “Cancel every data-sharing effort across the County.”
@graph.marin:feedback: One identified mismatch is a solvable design issue, not proof all sharing is impossible.

@graph.name: Schema leadership knowledge check

marin:gradeBands.name: A
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: Excellent. You can ask the questions that prevent another expensive “the systems integrate” surprise.

marin:gradeBands.name: B
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: Strong work. Make stable schemas and demonstrated mappings a normal part of your next project discussion.

marin:gradeBands.name: C
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: Good foundation. Revisit record matching and planned schema changes, then try another set of questions.

marin:gradeBands.name: D
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: There is progress to make. Start with the seven-question checklist; no programming required.

marin:gradeBands.name: F
marin:gradeBands.marin:message: No need to panic at the word schema. Read the guide again and begin with one simple question: “Are we talking about the same thing?”

@graph.name: Schemas: The Leadership Knowledge Check
@graph.abstract: Ten randomized questions about shared meaning, stable schemas, cross-system matching, responsible sharing, procurement, and executive habits.

@graph.name: County Leader’s Guide to Schemas
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Open with a normal leadership question: “How many times have we heard that two systems integrate, only to find out later they count different things?” Explain that a schema is not a programming test.

@graph.name: A Schema Is an Agreement
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Ask someone to describe an ordinary County form. Notice how field names and allowed values already express a shared agreement.

@graph.name: Same Field Name. Different Fact.
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Use People Served and work order statuses as two examples. Do not suggest that different departmental definitions are automatically wrong; what matters is recognizing the difference.

@graph.name: When Systems Exchange Information
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Transition to a practical question: how can different applications report one trustworthy story?

@graph.name: One Work Order, Two Systems
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Walk through a repair marked complete before its invoice is paid. Ask what “closed” should mean in a combined report.

@graph.name: Stable Does Not Mean Frozen
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: The phrase stable schema is not a request for outdated systems. It means planned changes and clear notice.

@graph.name: Which Record Is This?
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Emphasize that a matching name or address is not necessarily a reliable record match. Ask about work order IDs or other appropriate stable identifiers.

@graph.name: Someone Must Own the Meaning
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Ask who defines Case Closed in your current environment. Do not answer on behalf of a particular department.

@graph.name: Shared Meaning Is Not Blanket Access
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Technical interoperability and permission to share are separate approvals. Use a limited referral status as the example.

@graph.name: What Leadership Can Ask
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Tell participants that they do not need to read technical schemas. They do need to insist on understandable evidence.

@graph.name: Ask Vendors to Demonstrate
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Replace “It has an API” with “Show how it matches this particular County application and who supports changes.”

@graph.name: The 60-Second Schema Check
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Lead with the two memorable questions: “Does this have a stable schema?” and “Does this integrate well with the schema of our other application?” Encourage participants to use the full checklist in a meeting.

@graph.name: One Handoff Before a Big Promise
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Propose a small two-system exercise. The goal is a demonstration of field meaning, record matching, change handling, and approvals—not a countywide replacement project.

@graph.name: Make the Question Ordinary
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Reassure participants: a leader can ask for schema evidence and accept “we need to investigate” as a responsible answer.

@graph.name: Next Meeting: Ask for the Agreement
@graph.marin:speakerNotes: Close with one commitment: ask which fields mean the same thing, how the systems match, and who owns changes. Invite leaders to make schema a normal management word.

@graph.name: County Leader’s Guide to Schemas — Slide Deck
@graph.abstract: Fifteen discussion-oriented slides about shared meaning, stable definitions, evidence of integration, and better executive questions.
